lessons.title: Free pieces
lessons.body: Before anything clever, look for pieces your opponent left undefended. A loose piece is the easiest win in chess, and strong players never skip this check.
lessons.tip: Every move, ask: which of their pieces has no defender?

lessons.title: Checks, captures, threats
lessons.body: When you look for a move, look at the forcing moves first: every check, then every capture, then every move that threatens something. Forcing moves limit what the opponent can do, so they are easier to calculate.
lessons.tip: Scan in this order: checks, captures, threats.

lessons.title: Checkmate in one
lessons.body: Checkmate means the king is attacked and has no escape: it can’t move, block or capture. Look at the squares around the enemy king. Which are already covered? Then find the piece that covers the rest.
lessons.tip: Count the king’s escape squares before you give check.

lessons.title: The fork
lessons.body: One piece attacks two things at once. Your opponent can only save one. Knights are the best forkers: they jump, and nothing can block them.
lessons.tip: Look for two loose targets a knight-jump apart. A check in the fork is the strongest kind.

lessons.title: The pin
lessons.body: A pin freezes a piece in front of a more valuable one. If it moves, the piece behind is lost, or, with the king behind, it can’t legally move at all. Bishops, rooks and queens pin along lines.
lessons.tip: A pinned piece is a bad defender. Attack it again.

lessons.title: The skewer
lessons.body: A skewer is a pin turned around: the bigger piece is in front. When it steps aside, you take the piece behind it. King and queen on the same line are the classic target.
lessons.tip: Two enemy pieces on one line? Look for a skewer.

lessons.title: Discovered attack
lessons.body: Move one piece out of the way and the piece behind it attacks. The piece that moves is free to make its own threat, so the opponent faces two at once.
lessons.tip: Your pieces lined up behind your own pieces are loaded guns.

lessons.title: Double check
lessons.body: When two pieces give check at once, blocking or capturing can’t stop both. The king must move. It is the most forcing move in chess.
lessons.tip: A discovered check where the moving piece also checks is a double check.

lessons.title: Back-rank weakness
lessons.body: A king tucked behind its own pawns has no air. A rook or queen landing on the back rank can be mate. Many games end this way, even at club level.
lessons.tip: Give your own king a little air (one pawn step) before it’s too late.

lessons.title: Mate in two
lessons.body: Two-move mates usually start with a check or a sacrifice that drags the king or a defender to a bad square. Look at the final picture first: where could the mating piece land?
lessons.tip: Picture the mate, then work backwards.

lessons.title: Count attackers and defenders
lessons.body: A piece is safe only if it has at least as many defenders as attackers. Count both, cheapest attacker first. If you attack more times than they defend, you win it.
lessons.tip: More attackers than defenders means the piece falls.

lessons.title: Remove the defender
lessons.body: If a piece is guarded by exactly one defender, capture or chase away that defender first. Then what it guarded is loose.
lessons.tip: Ask what each enemy piece is defending, then take the defender away.

lessons.title: Trapped pieces
lessons.body: A piece with no safe squares is lost even before it is attacked. Knights on the edge and bishops deep in enemy territory get trapped most.
lessons.tip: Before chasing a piece, count its escape squares.

lessons.title: The sacrifice
lessons.body: Sometimes you give material to get more back: a bigger piece, a mating attack, or a pawn that promotes. A sacrifice is only good if you can see what comes back.
lessons.tip: Sacrifice for a concrete reason, never for hope.

lessons.title: Quiet moves
lessons.body: Not every winning move is a check or capture. A quiet move can set up a threat the opponent can’t meet. These are the hardest to find because they don’t shout.
lessons.tip: If nothing forcing works, look for a move that makes two threats.

lessons.title: Look at their last move
lessons.body: Every move changes something. Before your own plan, ask what your opponent’s last move attacks, and what it stopped defending. The last move is shaded on the board.
lessons.tip: What does their last move attack, and what did it leave behind?

lessons.title: Knight tricks
lessons.body: Knights move in an L and are the only piece that jumps. Their forks are hard to see because the targets are not on one line. A knight on e5 hits d7, f7, c6, g6, c4, g4, d3 and f3.
lessons.tip: Knights love to fork king and queen, or king and rook.

lessons.title: Promotion
lessons.body: A pawn that reaches the last rank becomes a queen. Often the whole idea is to clear one square for it, or to distract the only piece that can stop it.
lessons.tip: Count: how many moves to promote, and who can stop it?

lessons.title: Passed pawns must be pushed
lessons.body: A passed pawn has no enemy pawns in front of it or on the next files. Every step forward makes it more dangerous and ties down more of the opponent’s pieces.
lessons.tip: Push passed pawns with your pieces behind them.

lessons.title: Mate in three
lessons.body: Longer mates are chains of forcing moves. Keep checking until the king runs out of squares, and make sure every reply is covered.
lessons.tip: If every move is a check, calculation gets easy.

lessons.title: King hunt
lessons.body: When the king is chased into the open, keep checking. Each check gains time, and the king walks into your pieces.
lessons.tip: Checks buy time. Use them to bring in more pieces.

lessons.title: Smothered mate
lessons.body: When a king is surrounded by its own pieces, a single knight check can be mate. The famous pattern: queen sacrifice next to the king, rook takes, knight mates.
lessons.tip: A boxed-in king fears knights most.

lessons.title: Open files for rooks
lessons.body: Rooks are strongest on files with no pawns. Double them on an open file, then break into the seventh rank where the pawns and king live.
lessons.tip: Rooks belong on open files and the seventh rank.

lessons.title: The bishop pair
lessons.body: Two bishops cover both colours and work together across the whole board. In open positions the bishop pair is often worth an extra pawn.
lessons.tip: Have both bishops? Open the position.

lessons.title: Poisoned pawns
lessons.body: A free pawn can cost the game if taking it lets your opponent attack. Before you capture, ask what your piece leaves behind and how it gets back.
lessons.tip: Grab only when you can see the way home.

lessons.title: Develop, centre, castle
lessons.body: In the first ten moves: bring out knights and bishops, fight for the centre, and castle. Every move that does none of these is a lost tempo.
lessons.tip: Don’t move the same piece twice in the opening without a reason.

lessons.title: Opening traps
lessons.body: Early in the game, loose pieces and uncastled kings are everywhere. Many openings have traps where one careless move loses a piece.
lessons.tip: In the opening, check every capture for a trap.

lessons.title: The weak f7 and f2 squares
lessons.body: Before castling, f7 (f2 for White) is defended only by the king. Early attacks with queen and bishop often aim right there.
lessons.tip: Guard f7 and f2 until you castle.

lessons.title: King power
lessons.body: With the queens off, the king becomes a fighting piece. Bring it to the centre, where it attacks pawns and escorts your own.
lessons.tip: In the endgame, activate the king first.

lessons.title: The opposition
lessons.body: In king and pawn endings, when the kings face each other with one square between them, the side not to move usually wins the standoff. The other king has to give way.
lessons.tip: Kings face to face, one square apart: the side not to move has the opposition.

lessons.title: The rule of the square
lessons.body: Can the king catch a passed pawn? Picture a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the king can step into the square, it catches the pawn.
lessons.tip: Draw the square. Can the king get inside it?

lessons.title: Rook endgames
lessons.body: Rook endings are the most common endgame. Put your rook behind passed pawns, yours or theirs, and keep it active. A passive rook loses.
lessons.tip: Rooks belong behind passed pawns.

lessons.title: Knights and bishops
lessons.body: Knights are good when all the pawns are on one side. Bishops are better when pawns are on both wings. Put your pawns on the opposite colour to your own bishop.
lessons.tip: Pawns on both wings favour the bishop.

lessons.title: Queen endgames
lessons.body: In queen endings, checks are everywhere. Keep your king safe from endless checks, and look for forks: the queen attacks in eight directions.
lessons.tip: Queen endings: king safety first, then pawns.

lessons.title: Trade when ahead
lessons.body: When you are up material, trade pieces, not pawns. Every trade makes your extra material count for more.
lessons.tip: Ahead? Trade pieces. Behind? Trade pawns.

lessons.title: The blunder check
lessons.body: Before you play a move, take three seconds: what checks, captures and threats does it allow? Most lost games are lost to one missed reply.
lessons.tip: Before every move: what can they do next?

lessons.title: Candidate moves
lessons.body: Strong players list two or three candidate moves before calculating any of them. It stops you falling in love with the first idea.
lessons.tip: Find three candidates, then choose.

lessons.title: Calculate to the end
lessons.body: When a line is forcing, follow it until the position is quiet: no more checks or captures. Only then judge who is better.
lessons.tip: Stop calculating only when nothing is hanging.

lessons.title: Improve your worst piece
lessons.body: When there is no tactic, find your least active piece and give it a better square. Small improvements add up.
lessons.tip: No tactic? Improve your worst piece.

lessons.title: Name the pattern
lessons.body: You have met every pattern in this course. From here, puzzles come from all themes. Name the pattern before you move: fork, pin, skewer, discovery, back rank.
lessons.tip: Name the pattern, then play it.
